bibliographic.title: Enterprise-Scale Risk Decision Intelligence Systems Using Large Language Models (LLMs) For Automated Governance, Compliance, and Policy Enforcement
bibliographic.authors: B. M. Taslimul Haque; Md. Arifur Rahman
bibliographic.citation_apa: Haque, B. M. T., & Rahman, M. A. (2025). Enterprise-scale risk decision intelligence systems using large language models (LLMs) for automated governance, compliance, and policy enforcement. American Journal of Interdisciplinary Studies, 6(3), 254-305. https://doi.org/10.63125/te050f20

methodology.method_family: quantitative cross-sectional survey with descriptive statistics, correlation, multiple regression, CFA, and SEM (SPSS and SmartPLS)
methodology.sample_description: 400 governance professionals, compliance officers, cybersecurity analysts, enterprise risk managers, and operational executives employed in medium-sized and large enterprises across finance, healthcare, information technology, telecommunications, logistics, manufacturing, and insurance sectors
methodology.sector: finance, healthcare, information technology, telecommunications, logistics, manufacturing, insurance
methodology.technology_context: enterprise-scale risk decision intelligence systems using LLMs for automated governance, compliance, and policy enforcement

eligibility.decision_rationale: The provided text strongly supports LLM-based enterprise governance, compliance, and policy enforcement in regulated sectors, but does not evidence conversational AI, chatbots, agents, RAG, guardrails, or conversational governance mechanisms required for central fit to the review scope.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Python triage flagged conversational terms, but supplied excerpts contain no chatbot, agent, or conversational-system governance evidence; full-text verification is needed to adjudicate scope fit.

appraisal.notes: Appraisal is based only on abstract and partial introduction. Survey instrument details, recruitment, ethics approval, and limitations are not visible in the supplied text.

cerqual.explanation: Claims, constructs, and statistical methods are coherently described in the abstract, but only front-matter text is available; conversational-governance relevance is indirect, and ethics, limitations, and data-collection procedures are not evidenced.

coding.theme: Enterprise LLM governance for automated compliance and policy enforcement
coding.subtheme: Quantitative organizational adoption and performance outcomes

synthesis.main_claim: Enterprise-scale LLM governance systems significantly improve governance coordination, compliance reliability, institutional accountability, operational resilience, and predictive governance intelligence, with LLM capability integration positively predicting governance performance.
synthesis.contribution: Provides empirical survey evidence (n=400) linking LLM integration and related governance capabilities to enterprise governance and compliance outcomes across multiple regulated sectors.
synthesis.limitations: Supplied text does not report study limitations, ethics, instrument validation beyond reliability, or whether findings generalize beyond self-reported perceptions; conversational governance is not addressed.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as borderline or supporting evidence on enterprise LLM governance and compliance in regulated sectors; not suitable as central evidence for conversational governance without full-text confirmation of conversational-system mechanisms.

evidence.claim: Study uses quantitative cross-sectional design with 400 enterprise professionals across multiple sectors.
evidence.excerpt: A quantitative cross-sectional research design was adopted, and data were collected from 400 governance professionals

evidence.claim: Research focuses on LLMs for automated governance, compliance, and policy enforcement.
evidence.excerpt: enterprise-scale risk decision intelligence systems using Large Language Models (LLMs) for automated governance, compliance, and policy enforcement

evidence.claim: Sample spans regulated and high-stakes sectors including finance, healthcare, and insurance.
evidence.excerpt: across finance, healthcare, information technology, telecommunications, logistics, manufacturing, and insurance sectors

evidence.claim: LLM capability integration significantly predicts governance performance.
evidence.excerpt: LLM capability integration significantly influenced governance performance (β = 0.41, p < 0.001)

evidence.claim: Explainable AI implementation strengthens organizational transparency.
evidence.excerpt: explainable AI implementation significantly strengthened organizational transparency (β = 0.35, p < 0.01)

evidence.claim: LLM-driven governance systems support automated monitoring and intelligent policy enforcement.
evidence.excerpt: LLM-driven governance systems address these limitations by introducing contextual reasoning, semantic interpretation, automated monitoring, and intelligent policy enforcement

evidence.claim: No conversational AI, chatbot, or agent governance is evidenced in the supplied text.
Statistical analysis used SPSS and SmartPLS with CFA and SEM.
evidence.excerpt: Statistical analysis was conducted using SPSS and SmartPLS software packages through descriptive statistics, reliability testing, correlation analysis, multiple regression analysis, Confirmatory Factor Analysis, and Structural Equation Modeling

evidence.claim: Reliability analysis reports Cronbach's alpha from 0.87 to 0.93.
evidence.excerpt: Cronbach’s alpha values ranging from 0.87 to 0.93

evidence.claim: Ethics approval and study limitations are not reported in the supplied text.
